problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times {2i}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$

examples.knowledge_point: Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
examples.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $\,\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} X_i$ in the Cartesian plane given that $I = [-1,1] \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $X_i = \{ i \} \times [0, \, i^2].$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x \: : \: x \in A_k \:\:\textrm{for at least one}\:\: k \in I \big\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=-0.5,$ we have 

$$
X_{-0.5} = \{ -0.5 \} \times [0, 0.25] = \big\{ (-0.5,k) \: : \: k \in [0, 0.25] \big\}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(-0.5, 0)$ to the point $(-0.5,0.25)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/ccc75eac899efcab1d0b6fde12609a3ea8f61d6fec74c739ef3393fad32645a9.png)

In general,

$$
X_i = \{ i \} \times [0, i^2] = \big\{ (i,k) \: : \: k \in [0, i^2] \big\}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i, i^2).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/60c98be5d97748e9285bb5e9c30bba9781a5ef99245789718a7828b18a6df8fb.png)

 

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following figure that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} X_i{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/b3a61d686c78c76a4f461c1c771437d31030339b634661da8b8dc4f492db55eb.png)

feedback.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=N\times N$ in the Cartesian plane?
feedback.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=N\times N
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in N,\,y\in N}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any natural number.

$$
{S}_{1}={(1,y)\,:\,y\in N}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/34f779801b1bb52d5834ab4e04c91d92585af9876f5ea687ad59cb6931e0144c.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any natural number.

$$
{S}_{2}={(2,y)\,:\,y\in N}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/387709ae58ce7716338785f82e9159ce8570b046518554edd820c3ed31a23c53.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $N\times N$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/141d0b84041957cf8415db4673c999f5213ff23553e57ab7e0e9120e648f306c.png)
